fields.title: Vetka: Three Directions and One Year
fields.summary: Each direction asks for a budget and promises growth. Formulate a strategy and goals.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you bring to the board in three weeks?
fields.brief/role: You are Vetka's product manager, responsible for the entire product.
fields.brief/company: Vetka is a fictional subscription-based book reading app: 400 thousand monthly active users, 92% of revenue from subscriptions.
fields.brief/context: In three weeks, the board of directors approves the strategy and goals for the year. Three directions are asking for resources, each promising growth. Last year's goals were a list of features, and half were not released.
fields.brief/objective: Formulate the strategy, goals, and roles for each direction.
fields.brief/constraints: A team of 40 people. The budget will grow by 15% at most.
fields.brief/task: Choose what you will bring to the board and justify your choice.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Strategy is a list of rejections
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Until there is a single 'no' in the document, decisions will be made anew at every meeting, and whoever is loudest wins. Rejection is verified by numbers: 44% drop off at the second chapter versus 9% who mention the catalog—and buying new releases for half the budget is no longer obvious. The second rule is different roles: demanding revenue from a bet in a growing market means shutting it down before it has a chance to deliver.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Book subscription: 92% of revenue, mature market, market growth of about 4% per year.

Share of users who finished their first book is 31%. Those who finish renew their subscription 2.3 times more often.

Most drop off at the second or third chapter: 44%.

12-month retention is 39%.

Catalog: 62 thousand books. The largest competitor has 340 thousand. In surveys, catalog size is named as the reason for leaving by 9%.

Cost of sales: book rights are the main expense; there is bargaining for new releases, prices have been rising for the third year.

The copyright holder offers a package of new releases for an amount equal to half the annual budget for rights.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Audiobooks: the market is growing by 30% per year, our share is close to zero. Launched six months ago, 14 thousand listeners, revenue is 3% of the total. Cost per hour of recording is high, decreases with volume.

Social reading (discussions, clubs): not launched. The product team is asking for four people for a year. Demand is not validated: 38% in a survey said 'it would be interesting', but there are no signs in actual behavior.

Selling individual books without a subscription: has been running for two years, 4% of revenue, support and rights management cost more than it brings in. Mature market, small share. The decision to shut it down has been postponed for the second year.

Management attention is enough for about one new direction: last year we ran two, both progressed slowly.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Last year's goals: 'launch audio', 'build social features', 'redesign the home screen', 'increase engagement'.

Two out of four were achieved; no one could measure 'increase engagement'.

The bonus was tied to the number of active users; in the middle of the year, this was boosted with daily push notifications, after which notification opt-outs rose to 17%.

In meetings, audio is compared to subscriptions by revenue, and every time audio looks like a failure.

There is no vision; even within the team, people answer the question 'why do we exist' differently.

Any new idea seems equally appropriate, so the backlog grows faster than the team.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
The board wants 'ambitious goals' and 40% revenue growth.

One board member insists on buying the new release package: 'the catalog is what we are compared by'.

Another believes that audio is the future and we should invest there.

The CFO asks to finally decide the fate of individual book sales.

Last year's strategy was 30 slides long and did not contain a single rejection.

In conversations with readers, one thing is repeated: 'I buy a subscription, read the first book halfway, and that's it'.

40% revenue growth with 39% retention and current economics would require doubling acquisition.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: One bet, portfolio roles, outcome-based goals
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Formulate a vision and rejections, give directions different roles and requirements, and set goals based on outcomes with guardrail metrics.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
You base the vision on customer feedback: a person who hasn't finished a book in years starts reading regularly again. This rules out buying a new releases package for half the rights budget: only 9% leave due to the catalog, while 44% drop off at chapter two.
You rewrite the annual goal as an outcome: first-book completion rate from 31% to 40%, with notification opt-outs under 8% as a guardrail (last year they hit 17% for bonuses).
You define clear roles: subscription is for revenue and efficiency; audio is the single bet, measured by demand and cost per hour, not revenue; social reading is shelved as demand is unproven and focus is limited; retail sales are shut down as planned.
Instead of promising 40% revenue growth to the board, you show that with 39% retention, this would require doubling acquisition, and prove that book completion drives renewal by 2.3x.
Over the year, completion reaches 38%, retention hits 46%, and revenue grows by 24%.
Trade-off: the board's revenue target is missed, and debating this takes two out of three meetings.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Bring what the board asks for
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The board wants 40% growth, the catalog, and audio. Take on all three directions, buy the new release package, and set ambitious goals.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Half of the annual rights budget goes to the new release package. The catalog grows to 78 thousand—compared to the competitor's 340 thousand, the difference is still not in our favor.
Three directions are pursued simultaneously, but attention is only enough for one: audio slows down, social reading never leaves the design stage.
The 40% revenue goal is not achieved: with 39% retention, this would require doubling acquisition, while the budget only grew by 15%.
The share of users who finish books doesn't budge—no one worked on it.
By the end of the year, the board demands explanations, and there is nothing to explain: the strategy was once again a wish list.
Trade-off: agreeing to all requests resulted in a year without a single resolved issue.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The audio market is growing by 30% per year, the board member is right. Direct people and budget there, keep the core product as is.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Audio gets resources and grows: listeners reach 40 thousand, revenue share is 8%.
The cost per hour of recording decreases with volume, which is the right metric for a bet.
But the core product generates 92% of revenue and is left neglected: the share of users who finish their first book stays at 31%, retention at 39%.
Over the year, total revenue grows by 11%, almost entirely because the subscription didn't drop.
At the same time, the bet on audio is reasonable on its own and could pay off next year.
Trade-off: attention is given to a growing direction while the main leak remains untouched—44% drop off at the second chapter, and this is the cheapest thing to fix.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: The main problem last year was that goals were a list of features. Write proper, numerical goals for each of the three directions.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
Goals indeed get better: outcomes instead of tasks, numbers, deadlines, assignees.
This resolves some of last year's debates, and you remove the bonus tie-in to active users by adding a guardrail metric for opt-outs.
But goals are set for all three directions at once, and resources remain spread thin: attention is only enough for one, but now there are three sets of requirements.
At the same time, audio is expected to generate revenue on par with subscriptions—meaning a bet is evaluated as a mature product.
By the end of the year, two out of three goals are not met, leading to the conclusion that 'goals failed again'.
Trade-off: the format of the goals is fixed without choosing a direction; a good formulation does not replace a rejection.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: The goal is defined as work rather than an outcome, and is completed by releasing a feature
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: The strategy does not state where we do not play and what we reject
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: The same requirements are applied to all products in the portfolio
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: The vision does not rule out any good ideas, which means it does not work
